Because of this, we still want to run a pre-identification filter on each and every image this tool is run on in order to generate some metadata on it. We need to know: 1. Board material a. paper b. whiteboard c. chalkboard d. other 2. utensil a. pencil b. pen c. permanent marker d. dry-erase marker e. chaulk f. highlighter g. other 3. organization Are there many boards or just one? Are there a combination of types of boards? Because 1 & 2 are dependent on 3, that is if there is a white-board and a sticky note, we cannot definitively say which board type or utensil type is used, we must sub-divide images and form more of a json or yaml tree of what is happening, preferrably yaml. This requires that we find out the organization first and do it rather well. Let's look more in-depth at organization. Organization requires that the image be well understood, it shouldn't require the most amazing technology, but it shouldn't be super rudimentary either. Really as long as board area is detected, background noise can be cropped out or lose attention box bounds. Then within the attention box bounds, any sub-boards may be identified and noted. Generally they will be some form of rectangle, falling within the sizes of notecards, sticky notes, paper sizes, and folded or cut papers. They will not all be straight either so may require rotation, the camera fisheye may also have some effect here or I may just not have had a perfect andle and the board is scewed. turns.response_html:
That is a fantastic project concept. Managing a "second brain" across physical and digital media is a massive bottleneck, and Excalidraw is a great destination, but manual cropping is a soul-crushing chore.

To automate this cleanly, you are essentially building an Intelligent Document Layout Analysis (DLA) pipeline tailored for heterogeneous (mixed) media.

Because you want a tree-structured YAML metadata output and multi-image extraction, your idea of running Organization Detection first is mathematically and procedurally correct. You cannot classify the utensil until you have isolated the specific sub-board it is writing on.

Here is a architectural breakdown of how to build Milestone 1 (The Organization & Extraction Engine) along with the YAML schema to support it.

1. Architectural Strategy: The "Tracer Branch" Pipeline

To make this robust against skewed angles, camera fisheye, and heavy shadows, the pipeline should process each input image through four distinct stages:

[Input Image] 
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────┐
│  Stage 1:     │ ──► Drops perspective distortion & flattens main canvas
│  Global Prep  │ ──► Shadow-resilient binarization (Local Adaptive Thresholding)
└───────────────┘
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────┐
│  Stage 2:     │ ──► Finds contours of nested rectangles (papers, sticky notes)
│  Segmentation │ ──► Hierarchy tree generation (Parent canvas -> Child notes)
└───────────────┘
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────┐
│  Stage 3:     │ ──► Deskews & crops each individual sub-board
│  Extraction   │ ──► Outputs clean, raw-pixel sub-images
└───────────────┘
      │
      ▼
┌───────────────┐
│  Stage 4:     │ ──► Runs a lightweight vision model (or heuristic)
│  Classification│──► Populates the YAML metadata tree per node
└───────────────┘

Handling Your Edge Cases (Fisheye, Skew, Shadows)

  • Shadows: Traditional global thresholding (like Otsu's method) fails completely when a hand or head casts a shadow over a notepad. Instead, use Local Adaptive Thresholding (e.g., Sauvola or Bradley methods). This calculates thresholds based on small pixel neighborhoods, making handwriting pop out perfectly even inside a dark shadow zone.
  • Fisheye & Skew: Don't try to fix fisheye globally unless you have camera calibration data. Instead, handle it at the sub-board level. Once a bounding box is found, use a Perspective Transform (Homography) based on its four corners to "warp" it back into a flat, 90-degree rectangle. This automatically fixes both camera skew and minor lens distortion for that specific note.

2. The Target Metadata Schema (YAML Tree)

Since a single image can contain multiple boards (e.g., a whiteboard with three sticky notes stuck to it), the output metadata must be structured hierarchically.

Here is the proposed format for your system:

source_image: IMG_20260717_1200.jpg
timestamp: 2026-07-17T12:10:52Z
canvas_organization:
  type: compound_board # Options: single_board, compound_board
  total_extracted_notes: 3

# The root environment (the main background layer)
root_environment:
  board_material: whiteboard
  utensil: dry-erase-marker
  extracted_crop_path: ./output/IMG_20260717_1200_root.jpg

# All nested elements discovered inside the root environment
nested_notes:
  - note_id: 001
    board_material: paper # e.g., a standard yellow post-it
    utensil: permanent-marker
    geometry:
      bounding_box_tlbr: [120, 450, 620, 950] # Top-Left, Bottom-Right in original pixels
      rotation_deg: 4.5
    extracted_crop_path: ./output/IMG_20260717_1200_note_001.jpg

  - note_id: 002
    board_material: paper # e.g., an index card
    utensil: pen
    geometry:
      bounding_box_tlbr: [700, 1100, 1200, 1600]
      rotation_deg: -1.2
    extracted_crop_path: ./output/IMG_20260717_1200_note_002.jpg

3. Designing the Ground-Truth Test Cases

To build this without losing your mind verifying every image, you need a deterministic test harness. I recommend creating 3 baseline test cases that represent your real-world chaos.

For each test case, you should manually create a "Ground Truth" YAML file. When you write your code, the algorithm's output will be diffed against these files to check accuracy.

Test Case 1: The Clean Slate (Verification of Basics)

  • Visual: A single piece of white A4 paper laid flat on a dark desk, written on with a black pen. Minimal shadows, perfectly top-down.
  • Goal: Verifies that your pipeline correctly identifies a single_board, crops it perfectly to its boundaries, and doesn't hallucinate phantom sub-boards.

Test Case 2: The Multi-Note Compound (Hierarchy Verification)

  • Visual: A magnetic whiteboard containing text written directly on the board, with two square sticky notes (one pink, one yellow) stuck to it at slight angles.
  • Goal: Tests the parent-child hierarchy. The algorithm must output 3 images: the full whiteboard background, sticky note 1 (deskewed), and sticky note 2 (deskewed).

Test Case 3: The Real-World Chaos (Stress Test)

  • Visual: A notebook page shot at a sharp 30-degree angle under harsh overhead lighting, causing a strong diagonal shadow across the bottom half.
  • Goal: Tests the adaptive thresholding (shadow rejection) and the homography transformation (perspective warping). If the output image is square and legible, the tracer branch passes.

Next Steps

To move forward with building the prototype scripts for Milestone 1, what programing language or ecosystem are you planning to anchor this in? (e.g., a Python pipeline using OpenCV/Pillow, a Node.js backend, or leveraging an existing self-hosted vision model/LLM API?)

The application you are thinking of is almost certainly 3M's official Post-it® App. It is proprietary (not open source), but looking closely at its behavior, system requirements, and user feedback reveals exactly how it processes an image.

3M designed their system to recognize walls of notes simultaneously. To build your open-source, local-first alternative (note-distillery) for whiteboards, paper, and mixed media, we can reverse-engineer and adapt their core processing loop.

What 3M's Post-it App Does Under the Hood

The Post-it App works by capitalizing on strict geometric and color constraints. Because they manufacture the actual sticky notes, their algorithm uses shortcuts that our tool will need to make more flexible.

1. Multi-Spectral Color Segmentation (The "Shortcut")

Instead of trying to find edges in a monochrome image, the Post-it app looks for known, high-saturation color clusters (Post-it Canary Yellow, Neon Pink, Mint Green) against a neutral background (like a whiteboard or a wall).

  • The Math: They map the image to a color space like HSV (Hue, Saturation, Value) or LAB, where lighting shadows don't shift the "Hue" or "A/B color channels" drastically. They filter for those specific color bands to generate a mask of where the notes are.

2. Connected Component Labeling & Contour Fitting

Once they have a clean mask of the note colors, they group touching pixels together.

  • The algorithm runs a standard geometric check: Does this group of pixels have 4 distinct corners, and is its aspect ratio roughly 1:1 or 4:3?
  • If it passes, it gets a bounding box.

3. Layer Separation (Ink Extraction)

This is the clever part: The app doesn't just crop the photo; it often completely separates the ink from the paper background.

  • It analyzes the internal pixels of the note, calculates the average background color of the paper, and treats anything significantly darker (the pen strokes) as a vector-like foreground mask.
  • This allows the app to let users change the background color of the sticky note digitally while keeping their original handwriting intact!

Adapting This for # note-distillery (Milestone 1)

Because your pipeline needs to handle non-standard note sizes, chalkboards, and varying white pieces of paper, you cannot rely entirely on color range filtering. We have to make it more robust.

Here is the precise step-by-step process we need to build for your first tracer branch:

Step 1: Pre-Processing for Shadow Rejection

Instead of trying to find shapes in the raw image, create a temporary "detection canvas":

  1. Grayscale & Blur: Convert to grayscale and apply a slight Gaussian blur to clear out camera sensor noise.
  2. Adaptive Thresholding: Use a local adaptive threshold (like a 51x51 pixel window). This converts the image to pure black and white, completely eliminating large, sweeping shadows across a whiteboard or desk.

Step 2: Finding the Structural Layout (Contours)

Using the clean black-and-white mask, use a topological contour-finding algorithm (like OpenCV’s findContours with a hierarchical retrieval mode).

  1. Filter by Area: Ignore tiny specs (noise) and massive blocks (the room's background).
  2. Polygon Approximation: Run a Douglas-Peucker approximation on each contour. This reduces a wavy, hand-cut, or slightly wrinkled edge down to its core vertices. If a contour resolves cleanly to 4 corners, it is flagged as a candidate sub-board.

Step 3: Resolving the Hierarchy Tree (Parent vs. Child)

The contour discovery output naturally provides a tree structure telling you which shapes live inside other shapes.

  • Root Level: The largest detected boundary (e.g., the edge of the physical Whiteboard or Chalkboard).
  • Child Level: Smaller 4-corner polygons completely enclosed within the root boundary (e.g., index cards or sticky notes stuck to that board).

Step 4: The Transform & Extract (Homography)

For every valid child node found:

  1. Grab the coordinates of its 4 corners.
  2. Calculate a Perspective Transform Matrix that maps those skewed, rotated coordinates into a perfect flat rectangle (e.g., a crisp 500x500 pixel image).
  3. Apply that matrix to the original high-resolution color image, not the black-and-white detection mask. This ensures your final saved crop keeps its raw colors and maximum text clarity.

Setting Up Your First Test Target

To get this tracer branch off the ground, how do you prefer to run it? We can put together a focused script utilizing Python + OpenCV to handle the adaptive masking, contour tree sorting, and perspective warps.

turns.response_html:
Here are two distinct architectural plans of attack you can hand off to your local agents.

To give you a true head-to-head competition, Plan A focuses on traditional, predictable, ultra-fast computer vision, while Plan B leverages a local, deep-learning, object-detection approach. Both are designed to handle your requirement of parsing the organizational hierarchy first and outputting the raw, deskewed sub-images along with a YAML tree.

Plan A: The "Deterministic CV" Architecture

Focus: Pure Computer Vision (OpenCV, NumPy). High speed, low resource usage, mathematical predictability.

This plan relies on geometric features, edge gradients, and topological hierarchies to find notes. It treats the problem as a math puzzle of finding nested polygons.

The Implementation Steps

  1. Pre-Processing & Shadow Rejection: Convert the input image to grayscale. Apply a large-window Adaptive Thresholding (e.g., OpenCV adaptiveThreshold with a block size of 51 or 101) to completely eliminate gradients caused by harsh lighting or shadows, leaving a clean binary map of outlines.
  2. Hierarchical Contour Tree: Run cv2.findContours using the RETR_TREE retrieval mode. This automatically constructs a parent-child relationship tree of every enclosed shape in the image.
  3. Polygon Approximation & Filtering: Loop through the contour tree. For each contour, use cv2.approxPolyDP to simplify the edges. If it reduces to exactly 4 corners and its area falls within reasonable bounds (ignoring speckles and the literal room background), flag it as a candidate board or sub-note.
  4. Homography & Perspective Warp: For every validated 4-corner coordinate set, sort the points systematically (Top-Left, Top-Right, Bottom-Right, Bottom-Left). Calculate a target aspect ratio, then use cv2.getPerspectiveTransform and cv2.warpPerspective on the original high-resolution image to output a perfectly flat, deskewed rectangle.
  5. Heuristic Metadata Evaluation: Pass the flattened crops to a lightweight color/texture analyzer. (e.g., A high standard deviation in grayscale suggests paper/pencil; uniform color spaces suggest a whiteboard/marker; high dark-pixel density suggests a chalkboard). Output the final tree to YAML.

Strengths & Weaknesses

  • Pros: Runs in milliseconds; requires zero GPU; mathematically precise deskewing; perfectly predictable boundaries.
  • Cons: Can struggle if a sticky note's edge matches the whiteboard color exactly, or if a note is heavily wrinkled/torn (causing it to fail the "4 corners" rule).

Plan B: The "Deep-Learning Object Detection" Architecture

Focus: Modern AI (Ultralytics YOLOv8 / YOLOv11 nano). High flexibility, robust against edge noise, handles irregular shapes.

This plan doesn't care about perfect lines. It trains a small, highly efficient local neural network to locate notes based on what they look like texturally, rather than their exact geometric boundaries.

The Implementation Steps

  1. Model Setup & Training Data: Secure or mock a lightweight object detection model (like yolov8n.pt). The agent will define three bounding-box classes: canvas_root (the whiteboard/chalkboard), note_paper (sticky notes, loose sheets), and note_card.
  2. Inference with Confidence Maps: Pass the raw image directly into the model. The network will output bounding boxes along with class probabilities, completely bypassing shadow issues because the neural network learns to recognize text on paper regardless of the lighting gradient.
  3. Geometric Extraction via Segment Masks (Instance Segmentation): Instead of standard box coordinates, use a segmentation variant (YOLO-seg) to get a precise polygon mask of the detected note. Use a Rotated Bounding Box (OBB) calculation to find the minimum enclosing rectangle and determine its exact rotation angle ($\theta$).
  4. Affinity Transform Crop: Use the calculated rotation angle and center coordinates to build a rotation matrix via cv2.getRotationMatrix2D, rotate the canvas back to $0^\circ$, and crop the sub-note out of the high-resolution source.
  5. Model-Driven Metadata Generation: Because the model identifies the class explicitly during inference (e.g., detecting note_paper on top of a canvas_root whiteboard), the agent can dynamically stitch the hierarchical YAML structure together natively from the network's prediction array.

Strengths & Weaknesses

  • Pros: Unbelievably robust against wrinkled paper, non-rectangular notes, and overlapping notes; entirely unfazed by harsh shadows.
  • Cons: Requires a machine learning library setup (PyTorch/Ultralytics); takes longer to process per image; edge boundaries might occasionally be a few pixels off compared to exact mathematical lines.

Head-to-Head Comparison Framework

When both agents finish their tracer branches, have them run their pipelines against your 3 baseline test cases (The Clean Slate, The Multi-Note Compound, and The Real-World Chaos).

You can evaluate their codebases using this matrix:

MetricPlan A (Deterministic CV)Plan B (Deep Learning)Winner Criteria
Edge PrecisionExpecting pixel-perfect corner alignment.Might "close enough" the boundaries.Which crop has less background bleeding?
Shadow ResilienceRelies entirely on tuning the adaptive threshold.Inherent to the model's training.Look closely at Test Case 3's readability.
Speed / OverheadUltra-lightweight, native CPU.Requires model loading, heavier footprint.Milliseconds vs. Seconds per image.
YAML Tree AccuracyDerived from topological geometry tree.Derived from intersecting box coordinates.Does the nested hierarchy match reality?

Which approach do you personally think your local environment is better suited to spin up first?

Here is a systematic, production-grade engineering roadmap for Plan A (Deterministic Computer Vision). You can copy and paste this directly into a markdown file (PLAN_A_ROADMAP.md) for your agent to execute.

Roadmap: Plan A (Deterministic CV Architecture)

Objective

Build a local Python CLI utility using OpenCV, NumPy, and PyYAML to parse complex images containing single or multiple nested writing surfaces (canvases, papers, sticky notes). The pipeline must handle harsh shadows, lens skew, isolate each note into its own high-resolution, deskewed cropped image, and generate a hierarchical structural tree in YAML.

Phase 1: Test Harness & Local Environment Setup

Goal: Establish the ground truth data structure so the pipeline's output can be verified deterministically.

  • Task 1.1: Dependency Injection
    • Initialize a strict virtual environment (venv).
    • Lock dependencies: opencv-python-headless, numpy, pyyaml, and pytest.
  • Task 1.2: Establish Test Target Directory
    • Create a structured workspace directory layout: 
      note-distillery/
├── test_fixtures/
│   ├── case_01_clean/   (Single paper, flat, clean light)
│   ├── case_02_nested/  (Whiteboard parent + 2 sticky note children)
│   └── case_03_chaos/   (Extreme skew, heavy casting shadows)
├── output/
└── src/
  • Task 1.3: Author Ground-Truth YAMLs
    • For each test case, manually draft a expected ground_truth.yaml structure defining the expected layout type (single_board vs compound_board) and the count of expected extracted child crops.

Phase 2: Shadow Rejection & Binarization Pipeline

Goal: Ingest the raw image and produce a clean binary (Black & White) mask where shadows vanish and edges remain crisp.

  • Task 2.1: Pre-processing Filter Array
    • Ingest the high-resolution source frame.
    • Convert to grayscale (cv2.cvtColor).
    • Apply a gentle Gaussian Blur (cv2.GaussianBlur) with a small kernel (e.g., 5x5) to shed digital sensor noise without muddying high-frequency text lines.
  • Task 2.2: Local Adaptive Thresholding Engine
    • Implement cv2.adaptiveThreshold using ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C.
    • Crucial Parameter Matrix: Set a massive block size window (e.g., 51, 101, or dynamically calculated relative to short-edge image size) to reject expansive gradient shadows while holding tight onto structural element edges.
  • Task 2.3: Morphological Cleanup
    • Execute a structural closing operation (cv2.morphologyEx with MORPH_CLOSE) using a small rectangular kernel to snap open gaps in note borders caused by hand-drawn dashes or minor wrinkles.

Phase 3: Contour Tree Extraction & Polygon Approximation

Goal: Discover the parent-child geometry layout and confirm which nodes qualify as valid writing surfaces.

  • Task 3.1: Topological Tree Generation
    • Execute cv2.findContours passing RETR_TREE and CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE. This produces an explicit parent-child relational index tree array (hierarchy).
  • Task 3.2: Douglas-Peucker Polygon Approximation
    • Iterate through all discovered contours.
    • Calculate contour perimeter (cv2.arcLength) and simplify the curves using cv2.approxPolyDP with epsilon set tightly (e.g., 0.02 * perimeter).
  • Task 3.3: Geometry Filtering & Validation
    • Discard objects that do not resolve to exactly 4 coordinate points.
    • Apply min/max area filters to suppress background speckles or the extreme edges of the photo frame.
    • Map the valid 4-corner coordinates to their respective hierarchy parent IDs to distinguish between a root canvas (e.g., the whiteboard) and a nested node (e.g., a sticky note).

Phase 4: Perspective Transform & Extraction (The Crop Engine)

Goal: Take skewed, angled, or distorted regions from the original high-resolution image and square them off into flawless rectangular crops.

  • Task 4.1: Clockwise Coordinate Sorting
    • Write a deterministic point-sorting function. Take the 4 arbitrary polygon coordinates and consistently sequence them as: [Top-Left, Top-Right, Bottom-Right, Bottom-Left].
  • Task 4.2: Target Canvas Dimension Heuristics
    • Calculate the Euclidean distances between the sorted points to deduce the target physical aspect ratio (Width/Height) of the note. Set target pixel limits preserving original maximum pixel density.
  • Task 4.3: Homography Execution
    • Generate the conversion matrix using cv2.getPerspectiveTransform.
    • Apply cv2.warpPerspective back onto the untouched, high-resolution source color image to generate the final isolated note artifact without any edge filters applied. Export the crop to the designated target path.

Phase 5: Heuristic Material Analyzer & YAML Output

Goal: Synthesize spatial metrics and color spaces to build the final semantic data package.

  • Task 5.1: Material Classifier Heuristic
    • Analyze the pixel profile of each crop:
      • Whiteboard: High mean brightness, low saturation standard deviation.
      • Paper: Noticeable texture lines or specific HSV hue bands (e.g., neon yellow/pink for stickies).
      • Chalkboard: Low mean brightness, high color contrast to writing texture.
  • Task 5.2: Metadata Assembly & YAML Export
    • Map the structural hierarchy tree down into a clean nested dictionary.
    • Export the data package using yaml.safe_dump mirroring the schema target structure exactly.

Phase 6: Edge Case Resolution & Review

Goal: Stress-test the code against the ground truths and optimize edge cases.

  • Task 6.1: Run Head-to-Head Testing Verification
    • Validate script outputs against test_fixtures/ to verify structural validity and edge precision. Ensure the pipeline can run reliably on a local CPU in milliseconds.

Here is the systematic engineering roadmap for Plan B (Deep-Learning Object Detection & Instance Segmentation). You can save this as PLAN_B_ROADMAP.md for your second agent to execute.

Roadmap: Plan B (Deep Learning Architecture)

Objective

Build a robust local Python CLI utility using Ultralytics YOLO (v8 or v11), PyTorch, OpenCV, and PyYAML. This pipeline bypasses geometric pixel filters by using a deep-learning model to detect uneven, wrinkled, or low-contrast notes on a variety of surfaces. It will extract rotated bounding boxes or segmentation masks, compute rotation compensation, crop the sub-notes out of the high-resolution source, and map the overlapping/nested coordinates into a hierarchical YAML structure.

Phase 1: Test Harness & Synthetic Dataset Generation

Goal: Prepare a tiny local fine-tuning dataset and establish ground-truth metrics.

  • Task 1.1: Dependency Injection
    • Lock dependencies: ultralytics, torch, torchvision, opencv-python-headless, and pyyaml.
  • Task 1.2: Synthetic Annotation Strategy
    • Since a pre-trained model won't know the exact custom canvas types out-of-the-box, create a quick localized training set. Take 15–20 representative images of your notes.
    • Use an open-source local annotator (like Label Studio or CVAT) to annotate them with bounding boxes or polygons.
    • Classes to define: canvas_root (the main board background), note_paper (white paper, loose sheets, index cards), sticky_note (square colored notes).
  • Task 1.3: Target Schema Layout
    • Maintain the identical output structure as Plan A so that both agents' final YAML data packages can be compared programmatically.

Phase 2: Local Model Selection & Fine-Tuning

Goal: Initialize a lightweight vision model capable of running rapidly on a local CPU or standard GPU.

  • Task 2.1: Base Model Selection
    • Select yolov8n-seg.pt (YOLOv8 Nano Instance Segmentation) or yolov8n-obb.pt (Oriented Bounding Boxes). The Nano variants are chosen because they require minimal memory and execute inference locally in milliseconds.
  • Task 2.2: Fine-Tuning Execution Script
    • Write a localized training script (train.py) pointing to your custom YAML dataset config.
    • Train for a low number of epochs (e.g., 30–50 epochs) using standard augmentations (scale, mosaic, blur) to instantly teach the model to ignore strong overhead casting shadows and color gradients.
  • Task 2.3: Model Serialization
    • Export the finalized weights to a standalone deployment file (e.g., best.pt or optimized to onnx format for native CPU execution).

Phase 3: Spatial Inference & Coordinate Intersection Engine

Goal: Pass raw images through the model and resolve the physical layout hierarchy by comparing bounding boxes.

  • Task 3.1: Raw Inference Stream
    • Ingest the high-resolution source frame directly into the model without applying aggressive edge filters.
    • Extract the prediction array containing: Class IDs, Confidence Scores, and Bounding Box coordinates (xyxy or normalized polygon masks).
  • Task 3.2: Intersection over Union (IoU) Hierarchy Map
    • Because neural networks output flat arrays of detections rather than a geometric tree, write a dynamic parent-child engine.
    • Calculate the spatial intersection of coordinates. If a sticky_note or note_paper bounding box is geometrically contained within a larger canvas_root box, assign it programmatically as a child of that root canvas.

Phase 4: Deskewing via Rotated Rectangles

Goal: Read the exact angle of the neural net's selections and flatten the isolated elements.

  • Task 4.1: Oriented Box Extraction
    • If using Segmentation masks: Extract the contour coordinates of the mask using the model's output tensors. Pass the contour array to OpenCV's cv2.minAreaRect.
    • This function yields a data payload containing: (center_x, center_y), (width, height), angle_of_rotation.
  • Task 4.2: Affine Transformation Matrix
    • Construct an affine rotation matrix using cv2.getRotationMatrix2D based on the calculated center coordinates and the exact angle of rotation ($\theta$).
  • Task 4.3: Extraction Crop
    • Apply cv2.warpAffine to the entire high-resolution color source image to cancel out the rotation angle.
    • Crop the resulting aligned image using the target width and height metrics. Save the pristine raw-pixel image to the output bin.

Phase 5: Classifier Synthesis & YAML Serialization

Goal: Use the native class outputs of the neural network to write the finalized structure file.

  • Task 5.1: Inference-Driven Metadata Map
    • Translate the classification findings natively:
      • If class is canvas_root $\rightarrow$ assign board_material based on average base color features or split classes (e.g., whiteboard_root, chalkboard_root).
      • If class is sticky_note $\rightarrow$ assign board_material: paper.
  • Task 5.2: Structured Dump
    • Package the compiled JSON/dictionary data tree into the target YAML template via yaml.safe_dump.

Phase 6: Robustness Verification

Goal: Bench test against Plan A's outputs on chaotic, wrinkled, or high-shadow notes.

  • Task 6.1: Run Evaluation Benchmarks
    • Evaluate the script's performance against test_fixtures/case_03_chaos. Observe how cleanly it captures skewed note edges that are halfway obscured by shadows compared to the pure mathematics of Plan A.
